```{r options, include = FALSE}
knitr::opts_chunk$set(collapse = TRUE, comment = "#>", fig.width = 7.5,
                      fig.height = 4.6, fig.align = "center", dpi = 96)
old_options <- options(digits = 3, width = 90)
```

Latent class analysis (LCA) is a person-centred method for identifying
unobserved subgroups in data measured on categorical indicators (Collins &
Lanza, 2010). It assumes that the observations come from a small number of
unobserved classes, each characterized by its own probability of every
response to every indicator. Within a class, the indicators are assumed to be
independent of one another; this assumption of local independence means that
the classes alone account for the associations among the indicators. The
model estimates the response probabilities of each class, the proportion of
the sample in each class, and the posterior probability with which each
observation belongs to each class.

In learning analytics, LCA has been used to identify the engagement state of
each student in each course from indicators of online activity. In the
VaSSTra method, these states are subsequently arranged into sequences across
the courses of a programme, and similar sequences are grouped into
trajectories of engagement (López-Pernas & Saqr, 2023, 2024). Saqr and
López-Pernas (2021) and Saqr et al. (2023) applied this approach to the
engagement of students followed through a complete study programme, so that
the latent classes of single course enrolments form the building blocks of
students' longitudinal trajectories.

As with latent profile analysis, an LCA involves a sequence of decisions:
the number of classes, the estimation from multiple starting values, the
interpretation of the classes, the evaluation of the classification and of
local independence, and the relation of the classes to other variables
(Nylund-Gibson & Choi, 2018; Weller et al., 2020). This vignette presents a
complete single-level analysis in that order and extends the model to two
levels in the final section. In the output of this package the classes of
observations are labelled `profile_1`, `profile_2`, and so on.

```{r package}
library(latents)
set.seed(1)
```

The estimation uses random starting values; the seed is therefore set once
so that the results can be reproduced.

## Data

The `student_esm` data contain 2,582 experience-sampling reports from 100
university students, collected in a study of academic adjustment (Neubauer &
Schmiedek, 2024). At each report made when they had not studied since the previous prompt, a
student indicated whether they had been
engaged in each of eight activities since the previous report, and rated how
happy, relaxed, worried and exhausted they felt. The aim of the analysis is
to identify typical combinations of activities.

```{r data}
activities <- c("time_with_friends", "on_social_media", "tv_video_games",
                "listened_music", "sports", "walking", "reading",
                "part_time_job")
summary(subset(student_esm, select = activities))
```

Every activity is absent at most reports. Social media is the most frequent
(745 reports) and a part-time job the least frequent (103), so the classes
are distinguished by how far their probabilities of each activity exceed
these base rates.

The reports are nested in students. The first part of this vignette treats
each report as an independent observation, which corresponds to the
conventional single-level model; the nesting is taken into account in the
final section.

## Selecting the number of classes

The number of classes is not estimated by the model but specified by the
analyst, and is therefore chosen by fitting models with different numbers of
classes and comparing them (see the
[class enumeration](https://pak.dynasite.org/latents/articles/enumeration.html)
article). `enumerate_lca()` estimates models with one to six classes and
returns the results in one table.

```{r enumerate}
models <- enumerate_lca(student_esm, activities, n_classes = 1:6)
plot_enumeration(models)
```

```{r choose}
summary(models)
```

The BIC (Schwarz, 1978) is lowest for four classes, 13.2 points below the
three-class model. The fourth class, however, contains 1.3% of the reports
(about 32), which describe many activities at once, and the four-class model
reaches its best log likelihood from only one of its starting values. A
class of this size, supported by a solution that the starts do not
replicate, is weakly supported, and the ICL (Biernacki et al., 2000), which
additionally penalizes classification uncertainty, is lower for three
classes than for four. The ICL is lowest for one class, which has no
uncertainty to penalize, and among the models with more than one class it is
lowest for two; the two-class solution, however, has a relative entropy
below 0.5 and therefore separates the reports poorly. The three-class model
is retained.

## Estimation

`lca()` fits a single-level latent class model, estimated by maximum
likelihood with the expectation-maximization algorithm from multiple starting
values.

```{r fit}
fit <- lca(student_esm, activities, n_classes = 3)
fit
```

## Interpretation of the classes

The heatmap shows, for each class, the estimated probability that the
activity was reported.

```{r heatmap, fig.height = 3.4}
plot_profiles(fit, what = "heatmap")
```

The largest class, comprising 58% of the reports, is characterized by
screen-based activities: social media, television and video games, and
music. The smallest class, 4% of the reports, consists almost entirely of
reports of working at a part-time job. The third class, 39% of the reports,
has elevated probabilities of spending time with friends, walking and
sport, and a probability of social media use close to zero. The same
probabilities are shown below as profiles across the activities, with 95%
confidence intervals where the probability is not on its boundary.

```{r responses}
plot_responses(fit)
```

The probabilities with their standard errors. Several are estimated at zero
or one; a standard error is not defined on the boundary of the parameter
space, so those are held at their bound and have none.

```{r response-table}
head(get_results(fit, "responses"), 8)
```

## Classification quality

`diagnostics()` reports the classification measures and draws the four
classification plots: the effective size of each class, the distribution of
the posterior probability of each report's assigned class, each report's
contribution to the classification entropy, and the average posterior
probability matrix, which shows which classes are confused with which.

```{r diagnostics, fig.height = 3.6}
diagnostics(fit)
```

The relative entropy of 0.66 (Ramaswamy et al., 1993) indicates a moderately clear classification, although the reports of the
third class are assigned with an average posterior of only 0.71. Relative entropy describes the quality of the
classification for the chosen model rather than serving as a criterion for
the number of classes (Sorgente et al., 2025).

## Local dependence

The latent class model assumes that the activities are independent within
each class. The bivariate residual of a pair of activities compares their
observed co-occurrence within a class with the co-occurrence the model
implies, and a large value indicates a dependence the classes do not explain.
The p-value refers this Pearson statistic to a chi-square distribution that
ignores the estimation of the model's table, which makes it very conservative:
in one simulation from a correctly specified two-class model (n = 500, 200
replications) it rejected
0.25% of pairs per class, and 0.08% pooled, at a nominal 5%. `p_adjusted` is
corrected across all the pairs by Benjamini-Hochberg (Benjamini & Hochberg,
1995). A pair that passes the
filter below is therefore strong evidence of dependence, but a pair that does
not pass it is not evidence of independence.

```{r residuals}
subset(get_results(fit, "residuals"), p_adjusted < 0.01)
```

```{r residuals-values, include = FALSE}
residuals <- get_results(fit, "residuals")
largest <- subset(residuals, statistic == max(statistic))
stopifnot(nrow(largest) == 1L, with(largest, indicator_1 == "listened_music" &&
                                      indicator_2 == "walking"))
```

The largest residual is that of listening to music and walking in class
`r with(largest, sub("profile_", "", profile))` (`r with(largest, round(statistic, 1))`). `local_dependence`
names pairs of categorical indicators that are modelled jointly within each
class: the pair then has its own joint distribution in every class, and the
other activities remain independent given the class.

```{r dependent}
dependent <- lca(student_esm, activities, n_classes = 3,
                 local_dependence = "listened_music:walking")
get_results(dependent, "local_dependence")
```

The table gives each class's joint probabilities of the pair beside the
products of its marginal probabilities, which are the probabilities under
independence, and their ratio. The two models describe the same data and are
compared with `compare_models()`.

```{r dependent-compare}
compare_models(independent = fit, dependent = dependent)
```

```{r dependent-values, include = FALSE}
compared <- compare_models(independent = fit, dependent = dependent)
gain <- dependent$log_likelihood - fit$log_likelihood
added <- dependent$n_parameters - fit$n_parameters
lower <- with(subset(compared, delta_bic == 0), model)
```

The joint model raises the log likelihood by `r round(gain, 1)` at the cost
of `r added` parameters, and BIC is lower for the `r lower` model. The
dependence is present in the data, and the three classes describe the
activities about as well without modelling it.

## Classes and a distal outcome

`three_step()` estimates the mean of an outcome within each class. It uses
the BCH method, which applies the inverse estimated classification-error matrix
to modal class assignments (Bolck et al., 2004). These corrected
weights can be negative; posterior-probability weighting is the separate
`method = "proportional"` option. The outcome here is the happiness rating.

```{r three-step}
happiness <- three_step(fit, student_esm, outcome = "happy")
happiness
```

Happiness is highest in the class of reports away from screens (5.30 on
the seven-point scale), and lower in the screen-based class (4.63) and the
work class (4.53).

## Extension to two levels

Each student contributes many reports, so the reports are not independent.
When the student identifier is supplied as `id`, `multilca()` estimates a
two-level model: the classes of reports are estimated again, jointly with the student classes,
and need not coincide with the single-level classes; the students are in
addition grouped into latent classes that differ in the proportion of
their reports belonging to each class.

```{r two-level, message = FALSE}
two_level <- multilca(student_esm, activities, id = "student",
                      n_profiles = 3, n_group_classes = 2)
get_results(two_level, "profile_probabilities")
```

The two-level model is presented in detail in `vignette("lca")`.
